title: The Missing Pennies

post.author: u/workshop_nights_odgerel
post.title: I finish my late great-aunt's machines at night. The rowing club's expenses app tells a sculler to pay a man she never shared a cost with, and leaves him owed 3p that nobody owes.

blocks.text: My great-aunt, Winifrith Torvaine, built coin-operated machines for sixty years. In her last ten years she also wrote programs, the lists of steps a computer follows, for local clubs. She died in the spring and left me her workshop. I'm Odgerel. I program on night shifts and finish her work in the evenings. Each job still has its paper work order tied on with string.

blocks.title: WORK ORDER 57. Larkwater Rowing Club, autumn camp.
items: Members type in each shared cost, an expense, and the app shows who owes whom.
Split an expense equally, by exact amounts, or by percentage.
A Simplify button that turns it all into the fewest payments.

blocks.text: Winifrith built the app from classes. A class is a pattern for one kind of thing in a program, like a blank form: Group, Member, Expense. Each member has a balance: what they paid, minus their shares. A plus balance means the group owes you money; a minus balance means you owe the group.

Her old version split every cost two ways, and the halves always added back up. Three ways was new. £10.00 shared three ways came out as 3.3333333333333335 pounds a share, so I rounded every share down to whole pennies, two decimal places. Here are the program's steps, one per line:

Group.addExpense(payer, amount in pounds, split)
  shares: equal   = amount / count, rounded down to 2 places
          exact   = the amounts typed in
          percent = amount × percent / 100, rounded down
  payer.balance + amount
  each sharer: balance - share
Group.simplify()
  biggest minus pays biggest plus, repeat

Simplify works in steps. First it takes each member's balance, so many debts become one figure per person. That is called netting. Then the member who owes most pays the member owed most, as much as either needs. It repeats until nobody owes.

The camp ran from Sunday 11 to Friday 16 October. Mehmet, Taddeo, Zlatko and Domagoj row a four, steered by Sulpicia, the cox; they shared a cottage. Ilektra, Vasudha and Yoshiro are scullers, each rowing a one-person boat; they shared a caravan. No expense had someone from each crew in it. By Friday evening the app held 61 expenses.
At 21:52 tonight Ghislaine pressed Simplify. Each line is one payment, then what was left:

Ilektra   pays Mehmet    £292.26
Domagoj   pays Mehmet    £275.23
Sulpicia  pays Vasudha   £190.94
Zlatko    pays Mehmet    £171.59
Taddeo    pays Vasudha   £103.85
Taddeo    pays Mehmet     £67.09
Yoshiro   pays Mehmet      £2.51
left:     Mehmet owed £0.03, by nobody

At 22:03 Ilektra texted Ghislaine: she has never shared a single cost with Mehmet. Ghislaine added up the balances. Members are owed £1,103.50 and owe only £1,103.47. She emailed me at 22:20. Nobody has paid anything yet.
Every payment is right to the penny. Three of the pennies belong to nobody.
Beside the program, Winifrith's notebook has one line in pencil: *A penny will not cut in three.* Ghislaine wants the payments sent on Monday. What should I change?

blocks.label: expense_8_redrawn.png

diagram.aria: Expense 8, redrawn. Vasudha paid £10.00 for milk and bread, split three ways. Each share is rounded down to 3.33, and the three shares total £9.99. Vasudha's balance goes up by the whole 10.00 less her own 3.33, so plus 6.67. Ilektra and Yoshiro each go down 3.33, minus 6.66 between them. 1p is owed to Vasudha by nobody.

blocks.caption: I redrew expense 8 from the app. Vasudha paid £10.00 for milk and bread, shared three ways. Each share was rounded down to £3.33, so the shares add up to £9.99, but Vasudha's balance went up by the whole £10.00. So she is owed 1p that nobody owes: the odd penny left when 1,000p is divided by 3. Expense 22 (£25.00, three ways) and expense 34 (£63.21, five ways) each leave one more odd penny.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Start with expense 8. Write down the change to Vasudha's balance, then Ilektra's and Yoshiro's, and add the three. Do the same for expenses 22 and 34. All eight balances together should add up to exactly £0.00, because every penny someone is owed, someone else owes. Look at what kind of number your shares are, too. A number with a decimal point, kept the way most computers keep it, in base 2, is called a floating-point number, and most numbers with a decimal point can't be held exactly in one. Then list the expenses Ilektra shared and the ones Mehmet shared. Which of them is her £292.26 paying for? Last, Winifrith's line. When one of her machines took a coin it could not split, where did the coin go?

replies.author: u/workshop_nights_odgerel
replies.text: Ghislaine's first thought is to turn Simplify off: every share paid straight to whoever paid that expense, so each payment matches one receipt and nobody pays a stranger. She knows it means more payments. She hasn't counted them yet.

comments.author: u/nearest_penny_tvrtko
comments.text: Your bug is the rounding down. Rounding down only ever loses, so pennies can only vanish, and over 61 expenses they pile up. Round each share to the nearest penny instead: some go up, some go down, and across a whole camp they cancel out. Every shop till I've used rounds to the nearest penny. Leave Simplify alone; the fewest payments is what the club asked for.

replies.author: u/workshop_nights_odgerel
replies.text: Ilektra isn't the only one. Four of the seven payments run between someone from the four and a sculler.

comments.author: u/close_enough_malachy
comments.text: Money in floating point is never exact, so never test it against zero. Every program I've worked on compares totals with a tolerance: a gap small enough to count as equal. Check that the balances add up to zero within 5p, show them as balanced, and get some sleep. Nobody is going to chase 3p.

reply.prompt: Ghislaine wants the payments sent on Monday, and the club will use the app again. What should Odgerel change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Round each share to the nearest penny instead of down, so the odd pennies even out.
options.verdict: The same pennies, now both ways
options.part2: I changed rounding down to rounding to the nearest penny. On the bench the camp comes out exactly as before. £10.00, £25.00 and £63.21 each leave one odd penny, and a third or a fifth of a penny rounds down either way. The gap is still 3p, Mehmet is still owed 3p by nobody, and Ilektra is still told to pay Mehmet £292.26. Ghislaine didn't trust the list, so she worked out the camp's payments by hand on Sunday and sent those instead; nobody paid a stranger, and nobody was paid twice. On Saturday 7 November Yoshiro put the scullers' £20.00 head race entry into the app, split three ways: £6.67 each, which is £20.01, a penny more than he paid. On the bench the gap falls to 2p. It looks smaller, and it is two errors pointing opposite ways, one hiding the other.
options.senior: Rounding to the nearest penny is still rounding each share on its own, with nothing making the shares add up to the amount. When an amount doesn't divide evenly, no rounding of single shares can fix that: some penny has to go to somebody, by a rule you choose. Nearest-penny rounding only makes the error point both ways, so a total can look right while single expenses are wrong.

options.text: Keep money in whole pence, odd pence on the payer; net each pair who shared costs.
options.part2: I changed every amount and share to whole pence, kept as whole numbers: £10.00 is 1,000p. An equal split divides the pence, rounds down, and puts the odd pence on the payer's own share, so milk and bread is 334p for Vasudha and 333p each for Ilektra and Yoshiro. Every expense's shares now add up to its amount exactly. Settling up still nets, but one pair at a time: what each person owes the other from expenses they shared, minus what the other owes back, becomes one payment, listed with the expenses behind it. On the bench the camp needs 13 payments instead of 7, every one between people who shared costs, and the balances add up to exactly 0p. Ilektra pays Vasudha £194.03 for 11 expenses and Yoshiro £98.23 for 12. Ghislaine sent the list on Monday 19 October, and every payment had gone through by Wednesday; nobody was asked to pay a stranger, and Vasudha, Yoshiro and Domagoj each carried their own odd penny, as the rule says. On 7 November the head race came out at £6.68 for Yoshiro and £6.66 each for the others: £20.00.
options.senior: Count money in what actually changes hands: whole pennies, kept as whole numbers, so adding is exact. When an amount won't divide, give the odd pence to someone by a stated rule; then every expense's shares add up to its amount and every balance adds up to exactly zero, which a check can test. Netting is fine, but net where people can see why: one payment per pair who shared costs can list its own expenses. The fewest payments, made between strangers, save a few transfers and cost the members' trust.

options.text: Turn Simplify off and settle every expense on its own, so each payment matches a receipt.
options.part2: I switched Simplify off: every share is paid straight to whoever paid that expense. On the bench the camp needs 200 payments instead of 7. Zlatko and Domagoj make 33 each; Ilektra makes 19, £310.46 in all, and gets £18.20 back from the others for her two expenses. Each payer collects only the other shares, so the odd penny quietly stays with Vasudha, Yoshiro and Domagoj, and the balances add up to 0p. Every payment matches one receipt, and nobody pays a stranger. Ghislaine sent the list on Monday 19 October. The members spent the week sending each other small sums, and on Friday Ghislaine was still chasing the ones nobody had sent; no money went to the wrong person.
options.senior: Settling every expense on its own is exact and easy to check, because each payment matches one receipt. But it hides the rounding fault rather than fixing it: the payer happens to absorb the odd penny, and the code still has no rule that makes shares add up. And it costs effort, 200 transfers where 13, netted pair by pair, would do. Netting isn't the problem; netting between people who never shared a cost is.

options.text: Check that the balances add up to zero within a tolerance of 5p, and call that balanced.
options.verdict: Hides the gap until it grows
options.part2: I added a check: if all the balances add up to within 5p of zero, the screen says balanced. On the bench it says balanced, because 3p is under 5p. Everything else is the same: seven payments, four of them between people who never shared a cost, Ilektra told to pay Mehmet £292.26, and Mehmet owed 3p that nobody owes, now with no warning at all. Ilektra refused to pay a man she had never shared a cost with, so Ghislaine worked out the camp's payments by hand and nobody paid a stranger. On Saturday 7 November the scullers' £20.00 head race entry was split three ways and rounded down to £6.66 each. The gap became 5p, the check said NOT balanced, and Ghislaine emailed me again.
options.senior: A tolerance suits measurements that can never be exact, such as a temperature. Money counted in pennies can be exact, and a ledger should add up to exactly zero; a check that allows 5p allows every mistake smaller than 5p, and small mistakes add up. Python's own documentation prefers decimal arithmetic for accounting, where equality must hold exactly. Fix how money is stored, then check for zero.

sim.title: Run the camp's expenses through the app
sim.lede: You're Odgerel at the workbench, replaying Larkwater's camp from Sunday 11 October 2026, before the first expense. Eight members: the four and its cox (Mehmet, Taddeo, Zlatko, Domagoj, Sulpicia) and three scullers (Ilektra, Vasudha, Yoshiro); no expense has someone from each crew. 61 expenses come in by Friday evening, each split equally, by exact amounts or by percentage. The payer's balance goes up by the amount, and each sharer's goes down by their share. At the end the app settles up, at 21:52 on Friday. Change the design: as built (each share rounded down to the penny, in pounds, then Simplify), rounded to the nearest penny, as built with a check that calls a gap under 5p balanced, every expense settled on its own, or whole pence with the odd pence on the payer's share and one netted payment per pair who shared costs. Add a later expense, the scullers' £20.00 head race entry on Saturday 7 November, to the same books; payments made in between change no gap.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press Step eight times and watch expense 8, milk and bread, open a gap of 1p. Run the camp: a 3p gap, 7 payments, and Ilektra told to pay Mehmet. Try the nearest penny, then add the head race and read the gap. Try the check with and without the head race. Then settle every expense on its own and count the payments. Last, whole pence, and read who Ilektra pays.

explain.oneLine: Nothing has left anyone's pocket. Each uneven share was rounded down while the payer was still credited the whole amount, so three odd pennies ended up owed by nobody; then Simplify netted everyone's balances together, and payments ran between people who never shared a cost.

steps.title: Where the 3p came from.
steps.text: First, Vasudha paid £10.00 for milk and bread, shared three ways. Second, the program divided 10.00 by 3 and got 3.3333333333333335: a floating-point number, kept in base 2, which can't hold a third, or most decimal fractions, exactly. Third, it rounded each share down to 3.33, so the three shares came to £9.99. Fourth, it still added the whole £10.00 to Vasudha's balance. Her balance went up by £6.67 (10.00 less her own 3.33), while Ilektra's and Yoshiro's went down by £6.66 between them: 1p owed to her by nobody. Expense 22, £25.00 three ways, and expense 34, £63.21 five ways, did the same, for 3p in all. What went wrong at each step: an amount that doesn't divide, a number that isn't exact, a rounding with no rule for the odd penny, and a payer credited more than the shares add up to.

steps.title: Why never before, and why only 3p.
steps.text: Winifrith's version split every cost two ways. Halving a number is always exact in base 2, so her two halves always added back up to the amount. Three-way and five-way splits were new this camp. Most of the 61 expenses divide evenly: whole pounds split five ways, or amounts such as £13.50 split three ways. Only an amount whose pence leave a remainder loses anything: 1,000p divided by 3 leaves 1p. Rounding to the nearest penny would have lost the same three pennies, because a third or a fifth of a penny rounds down either way.

steps.title: Model money as whole pence, with a rule for the odd ones.
steps.text: A Group holds Members and Expenses. An Expense has a payer, an amount and a Split. A Split has one job: turn an amount into shares that add up to it exactly. Its steps: first, divide the pence by the number of sharers and round down; second, count the odd pence left over; third, give them out by a stated rule, here onto the payer's own share. Equal, exact and percentage splits all finish with that same last step, so every kind of split keeps the promise. The ledger, the record of everyone's balance, then adds the amount to the payer and takes each share from its sharer, so it adds up to zero after every expense, which a check can test exactly. What can go wrong: a new kind of split that rounds on its own and skips the rule.

steps.title: Netting gives few payments, not clear ones.
steps.text: Simplify nets in two steps: add up each member's balance, then pair the biggest minus with the biggest plus, again and again. The money comes out right, because netting never changes anyone's total. But it forgets who shared what: the four's debts and the scullers' credits are just numbers in one pot, so two of the four paid Vasudha, and two scullers paid Mehmet. Netting one pair at a time keeps the reason. For Ilektra and Vasudha: add what Ilektra owes from Vasudha's expenses, subtract what Vasudha owes from Ilektra's, and send the difference, listed with the 11 expenses behind it. That gives 13 payments instead of 7, every one between people who shared costs. What can go wrong: in a big group where everyone shares with everyone, pairs multiply, and netting the whole group may be worth its puzzles.

steps.title: The fix, step by step.
steps.text: First, store every amount and share as whole pence, kept as whole numbers. Second, give Split one method that turns an amount into shares, with the odd pence on the payer's share, and make every kind of split call it. Third, after every expense, check that its shares add up to its amount and that all balances add up to exactly 0p, with no tolerance. Fourth, settle up one pair at a time, each payment listed with its expenses. What can go wrong: amounts already stored in pounds must be turned into pence once, by rounding each to the nearest penny, because 63.21 kept in base 2 may sit a hair away from 63.21, and rounding down could then lose a penny.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for the scullers. Expense 8, 1,000p paid by Vasudha, goes to Split.shares, which gives 333, 334 and 333 pence, the odd penny on Vasudha's own share. The ledger's balances total 0p. Settling up nets each pair who shared costs: Ilektra pays Vasudha £194.03 for 11 expenses, Ilektra pays Yoshiro £98.23 for 12, Yoshiro pays Vasudha £100.75 for 19. The four's 10 pairs settle the same way.

notes.text: the four's 10 pairs settle the same way

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for the scullers. Expense 8 is 1,000p; Split.shares gives 333p, 334p and 333p, with the odd penny on Vasudha's own share, so the shares add up to the amount and the ledger's balances total exactly 0p. Settling up nets each pair who shared costs and lists the expenses behind each payment: three payments for the scullers, ten for the four, 13 in all.

fix.title: The fix: whole pence with an odd-pence rule; one netted payment per pair
fix.text: Store money as whole pence, kept as whole numbers, so adding is exact. Give Split one method that divides the pence, rounds down, and puts the odd pence on the payer's own share; every kind of split, equal, exact or percentage, finishes through it. After every expense, check exactly that the shares add up to the amount and the balances to 0p. Settle up one pair at a time: what each person owes the other from expenses they shared, netted into one payment, listed with those expenses. Turn stored pounds into pence once, rounding each to the nearest penny.

limits: Whole pence make the books add up; they don't make the odd pence fair. Here the payer always carries them, up to 2p on a three-way split and 4p on a five-way one. Some groups rotate who gets them; either way, write the rule down.

Listing the expenses behind a payment trades against privacy. Splitwise declined to show the details behind its simplified payments, saying "you shouldn't be able to see the details of a transaction between Y and Z". Pair netting avoids that, because both people shared every expense listed.

Netting pair by pair takes more payments than netting the whole group: 13 here against 7. In a big group where everyone shares with everyone, the pairs multiply, and netting the whole group, with its puzzling payments, may be the better deal.

explain.seniorTake: Model money as what really changes hands: whole pennies, in whole numbers. Never let a division decide on its own where a penny goes; give every remainder to somebody by a written rule, and test after every expense that the shares add up to the amount and the ledger to exactly zero. Floating point is for measurements; a tolerance in a ledger is a place for mistakes to hide. Then treat simplifying debts as a design choice with a cost: netting the whole group gives the fewest payments, and loses the reason for each one. People pay what they understand. Net within the people who shared the costs, and let each payment show what it settles.

realWorld.title: Python: most decimal fractions aren't exact in base 2
realWorld.text: The Python tutorial's chapter on floating-point arithmetic says: "Unfortunately, most decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly as binary fractions." Its example: 0.1 + 0.1 + 0.1 == 0.3 gives False. It adds: "For use cases which require exact decimal representation, try using the decimal module which implements decimal arithmetic suitable for accounting applications and high-precision applications."

realWorld.title: Python's decimal module: exact for money, still rounding
realWorld.text: The decimal module's documentation says "Decimal numbers can be represented exactly" and "The exactness carries over into arithmetic." Of binary floating point it says the small differences "prevent reliable equality testing and differences can accumulate. For this reason, decimal is preferred in accounting applications which have strict equality invariants." It still rounds: quantize() "is useful for monetary applications that often round results to a fixed number of places", which is why the odd-pence rule is needed anyway.

realWorld.title: Splitwise: what Simplify Debts does
realWorld.text: Splitwise's help article says Simplify Debts "restructures who owes whom within a group" and "It never changes anyone's total balance". Its own example ends: "Everyone ends up at the same place, with one fewer payment." The total each person owes stays right; who pays whom is what changes.

realWorld.title: Splitwise, 2013: why it doesn't show the details
realWorld.text: Asked in 2013 to show what lay behind a simplified payment, Splitwise support said it does not save the full details, because "you shouldn't be able to see the details of a transaction between Y and Z". Netting the whole group and explaining each payment pull against each other.

asked: Design Splitwise: an app for sharing expenses in a group.
How would you store money, and how do you split £10.00 three ways?
How do you simplify debts, and what does it cost?
interview.answer: Start with the model. A Group has Members and Expenses. An Expense has a payer, an amount and a Split; the split can be equal, exact amounts or percentages, and each kind turns the amount into one share per sharer. A ledger keeps each member's balance: the payer goes up by the amount, each sharer down by their share. Store money as whole minor units, pence or cents, in integers, never as floating point, which can't hold most decimal fractions exactly. Every split must produce shares that add up to the amount: divide, round down, and hand out the remainder by a stated rule, for example on the payer's share or one each to the first sharers in a fixed order, so £10.00 three ways is 334, 333 and 333 pence. Then assert after every expense that the shares sum to the amount and the balances to exactly zero, with no tolerance. For settling up, netting each member's balance and repeatedly pairing the biggest debtor with the biggest creditor gives at most one payment fewer than the number of members, but it pairs people who never shared a cost and can't explain why. Netting per pair who shared costs gives more payments, each traceable to its expenses. Mention that finding the true minimum number of payments is a much harder search, multiple currencies are settled separately, and expenses must be edited or deleted without breaking the ledger.

A widely used programming language. Its documentation is quoted here on floating-point numbers and decimal arithmetic.
A payment between two members who were never in the same expense, as payer or sharer.
What members are owed minus what members owe, in pence. It should be 0p; as built it is 3p after the camp.
Odgerel's workbench: the sim, which replays the camp's 61 expenses through whichever design you pick.

atWork: Look for money kept as floating-point numbers: price, amount or balance fields typed as float or double in code, or as a float column in a database. Read-only access to the code is enough. Then look for every place a total is divided: splitting a bill, a discount spread over items, tax on lines, a refund shared out. Ask of each one: do the parts add up exactly to the whole, and if not, who gets the remainder, by what written rule? A check that compares money with a tolerance, such as abs(a - b) < 0.01, is a sign the representation is wrong. Store whole minor units (pence or cents) as integers, or use a decimal type, put the remainder rule in one shared function, and add an exact check that the parts sum to the whole. Where your product nets debts or payments, check whether each payment can be explained to the people in it.

recall.prompt: Three flatmates share £1,000.00 of rent each month in an app that keeps money as decimal numbers in pounds and rounds each share down to two places. After a year, the flatmate who pays the landlord is owed 12p that nobody owes. What is happening, and what do you change?

keyIdeas.idea: Each month the shares come to a penny less than the rent, but the payer is credited the whole rent: one penny a month owed by nobody
Keep money in whole pence and give the odd pence to someone by a stated rule
Check exactly that the shares add up to the amount and the balances to zero, with no tolerance

recall.model: Each month the app divides £1,000.00 by 3, gets 333.333..., and rounds each share down to £333.33. The three shares add up to £999.99, a penny short, but the payer's balance goes up by the whole £1,000.00, so a penny a month is owed by nobody: twelve over a year. Keep money in whole pence, as whole numbers: 100,000p divided by 3 is 33,333p with 1p left over, and that odd penny goes to someone by a stated rule, for example onto the payer's own share. Then check after every split that the shares add up to the amount and the balances to exactly zero, with no tolerance.

recall.prompt: Vasudha pays £10.00, split equally three ways. The app rounds each share down to £3.33 and adds the whole £10.00 to Vasudha's balance. What do the three balances add up to?
options: +£0.01: a penny owed to Vasudha that nobody owes
-£0.01: a penny owed by Ilektra and Yoshiro to nobody
+£0.03: a penny for each of the three shares
recall.why: Vasudha goes up by 10.00 and down by her own 3.33: +6.67. Ilektra and Yoshiro go down by 3.33 each: -6.66. Together that is +0.01. The shares came to £9.99 while the payer was credited £10.00, so the odd penny is owed to her and owed by nobody.

recall.prompt: An office lunch app adds up all twelve staff members' balances and has the biggest debtor pay the biggest creditor, again and again. A new starter, who has only ever had lunch with the post room, is told to pay the finance director, whom she has never eaten with. Is the money wrong? Why does it happen, and how would you change the settling up?

keyIdeas.idea: The money is right: netting keeps everyone's total, it only changes who pays whom
Netting the whole office in one pot forgets who shared which costs, so payments can join strangers
Net one pair at a time, between people who shared costs, and list the expenses behind each payment

recall.model: The money is right: netting keeps each person's total and only changes who pays whom, so the new starter pays exactly what she owes. But adding up everyone's balance in one pot forgets who shared which costs, and the biggest debt meets the biggest credit even when the two never shared a lunch. Settle one pair at a time instead: for each pair who shared costs, what each owes the other, netted into one payment, with a list of the lunches behind it. It takes a few more payments, and each one explains itself.

recall.prompt: Which change makes every expense's shares add up to its amount exactly?
options: Round each share to the nearest penny instead of down
Keep whole pence and put the odd pence on the payer's share
Accept any gap under 5p as balanced
Store each share as a percentage instead of an amount
recall.why: Only a rule for the remainder makes the parts add up: £10.00 three ways becomes 334p for the payer and 333p each for the others. Rounding to the nearest penny still loses a penny on £10.00 three ways; a tolerance hides the gap; a percentage still has to be turned into pence and rounded.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. Whole pence, the payer's odd pence and one payment per pair have worked since October; every balance has added up to exactly 0p. This month Wawrzyniec, the club's new volunteer, added a new kind of split, by portions, so a rower who eats double pays double. He wrote it as its own class, PortionSplit: each share is the amount times that person's portions, divided by all the portions, then rounded to the nearest penny. On Saturday 9 January, at the winter training day, the app refused to save a £10.00 pizza shared at 1, 1 and 1 portions. The exact check said the shares came to £9.99.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did the new split break the rule the old ones keep, and how should PortionSplit be written so the next new kind of split can't do the same?

keyIdeas.idea: PortionSplit rounds each share on its own and has no odd-pence rule, so its shares don't add up to the amount
Put the whole-pence rule in one place that every kind of split uses
The exact check did its job by refusing the expense; keep it, with no tolerance

coldCase.model: PortionSplit rounds each share on its own, with no rule for the odd pence: 10.00 times a third is 3.333, which rounds to 3.33 three times, so the shares don't add up to the amount and lost a penny, the same fault as the camp's. The old splits keep the rule because they all finish through Split's one method that hands out the odd pence. Put that rule in one place and make every kind of split use it: PortionSplit should work out each share in pence, round down, then pass the odd pence to the same method, so the payer's share takes them. The exact check did its job: it refused the expense before a wrong penny reached the books. Keep it, with no tolerance.
